newsitem.title: UK: INLA guerrillas admit killing N.Ireland policeman.
newsitem.headline: INLA guerrillas admit killing N.Ireland policeman.

text.p: A small Irish Catholic guerrilla group said on Saturday it had killed an off-duty Northern Ireland policeman in a crowded Belfast bar on Friday night.
The Irish National Liberation Army (INLA) called the BBC to say it had gunned down 24-year-old Darren Bradshaw at close range in the city centre's Parliament Bar.

Bradshaw, serving with the predominantly Protestant Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC), was the first policeman to be killed since the larger Irish Republican Army (IRA) ended a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996 and resumed its guerrilla campaign to end British rule in Northern Ireland.
A caller using a recognised codeword telephoned the BBC in Belfast and said that he was speaking on behalf of the INLA.
"We executed the policeman last night in the Parliament Bar," he said. The IRA denied any involvement in the killing.
The shooting and recent sectarian attacks have cast a cloud over hopes that last week's election of a new British Labour government might revive the province's paralysed peace process.
The INLA attack also raised fears about whether an already shaky truce declared by Protestant pro-British "Loyalist" guerrillas would hold.
On Thursday, a Catholic man died 12 days after being savagely kicked by a Loyalist mob in the town of Portadown.
Tony Worthington, a minister in Britain's Northern Ireland Office, said the killing of the policeman was an outrage.
"For its part this government reaffirms it will never give way or be deflected from its course by politically-motivated violence, from wherever it comes," he said in a statement.

Britain and Ireland say dialogue is the key to solving Northern Ireland's deep-seated communal and political ills but insist the IRA must declare a fresh ceasefire before its political wing Sinn Fein is given a place at all-party talks.

The INLA, a small organisation with a bloody record, was formed in 1975 and has been blamed for a number of shootings over the past year. In recent years it has been racked by a power struggle and bloody internal feuds.

In 1979 it won worldwide notoriety by killing British member of parliament Airey Neave, a close friend of Margaret Thatcher, who later became British prime minister. He died when a bomb blew up his car near the British parliament.
In 1982 INLA guerrillas blew up a discotheque in the Northern Ireland garrison town of Ballykelly in County Londonderry, killing 17 off-duty soldiers and civilians.
